bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
bivy.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
bivy.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
bivy.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
bivy.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
bivy.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.

This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek highway pullout, for Mount Hardy's south face
bivy.notes: This is the short way up Mount Hardy and the reason most parties never carry a pack up the PCT for it at all: about four and a half miles and four thousand one hundred feet, done comfortably in a day. Walk west along the highway across Swamp Creek, leave the road and climb north and north-east through timber to gain the prominent ridge on the south side of the peak, then follow the south face, which is largely a walk with occasional easy scrambling on loose talus. It is a different trip entirely from the PCT approach and needs no camp, so it is included here as the honest alternative rather than as a site anyone would choose to sleep at. Parties wanting Hardy together with Golden Horn and Tower should use the PCT and the Snowy Lakes or Methow Pass camps instead; parties wanting Hardy alone should start here.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek itself, immediately below the road, and further water on the lower slopes. None higher on the south face.
bivy.permit: None to stop here. The land is national forest and no camping permit applies. Whether an overnight in a highway pullout is welcome varies, so the uncontroversial answer is to sleep at one of the developed campgrounds east of Washington Pass and drive over in the morning, or to sleep in the Rainy Pass lot.
bivy.capacity: A widened shoulder on SR 20 a couple of miles west of Rainy Pass, just east of Swamp Creek. Room for a few cars. This is a roadside start, not a camp — there are no facilities of any kind.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/interagency pass required at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead self-pay station (Northwest Forest Pass day fee is about $5/vehicle).
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; camp on durable/existing sites at Snowy Lakes. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft in the adjoining Pasayten Wilderness, and Snowy Lakes camp (~6,700 ft) sits well above that line, so plan on a stove only.
access.permit: A free self-issue Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead kiosk) is required for overnight camping along this Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest corridor, including Snowy Lakes camp. This is separate from the PCT long-distance permit, which is only needed for continuous PCT thru-hikes of 500+ miles.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and the Silver Star Mountain gate (MP 171), a span that includes both Rainy and Washington Passes - typically early December through mid-April/May.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA; (509) 996-4000); the approach runs along the southern edge of the Pasayten Wilderness.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day at the Rainy Pass trailhead (cash/check or digital day pass); Northwest Forest Pass and Interagency (America the Beautiful) passes also honored.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambling.
access.closures: Entire approach is inaccessible whenever SR 20 is under its winter closure (roughly late Nov through late Apr/mid-May); confirm current road status with WSDOT before driving in.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Winthrop, WA)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee at Rainy Pass trailhead

bivy.name: Gorge Creek overlook, the trailhead you sleep at
bivy.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.
bivy.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
bivy.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
bivy.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
bivy.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. THE OBVIOUS CLOSER OPTION IS GONE: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.
bivy.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
bivy.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.

bivy.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
bivy.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.
bivy.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.

bivy.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
bivy.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. NOTE THE OTHER APPROACH: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
bivy.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.
bivy.capacity: Room for about two small tents on a snow ledge by the saddle. That is the whole capacity, and it is not a place to plan on sharing.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; this is an off-trail route with no established campsites - camp on durable surfaces (rock, snow, or gravel) where possible. NPS backcountry rules require cross-country camping at least 1/2 mile from any maintained trail and out of sight of it. A permit is required only for overnight camping, not for a single-day scramble.
access.permit: No permit is needed for a day scramble. A NPS Wilderness Permit is required for overnight camping: reserve on Recreation.gov, watch the mandatory orientation video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Summer-season (mid-May-early October) backcountry camping fees are $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (youth 15 and under free); no camping fee is charged early October-mid-May.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for the season in late November/early December and typically doesn't fully reopen until mid-to-late April (sometimes May in heavy-snow years) - check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report before driving. The Gorge Creek Overlook/Diablo trailhead area sits between the highway's two winter closure gates (Newhalem, milepost 120, and Ross Dam Trailhead/Silver Star, milepost 134/171), so it is among the first sections to lose road access as the highway closes and one of the last to reopen. The alternate Stetattle Creek Trail (the north/west approach via Diablo) is fully closed as of 2026 - not just historically closure-prone - due to standing dead trees and debris from the 2023 Sourdough Fire; NPS lists the entire trail under its current fire-closures page. Do not plan on this alternate approach until NPS lifts the closure; use the standard Gorge Creek Overlook approach instead.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None. Davis Peak's trailheads (Gorge Creek Overlook, Stetattle Creek/Diablo) are within North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area, which charges no entrance fee and requires no day-use parking pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is only needed at trailheads on adjacent national forest land elsewhere along SR 20 (e.g., Rainy Lake, Blue Lake near Washington Pass) - not at this trailhead.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass ($5/day equivalent) for trailhead parking; the wilderness permit itself is free to obtain in person at Marblemount, though Recreation.gov charges a small fee for advance-reserved permits
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Backcountry wilderness permit required for camping, issued by the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount for the Inspiration zone
access.closures: Cascade River Road is gated and closed to vehicles in winter; check NPS road-conditions page for current washout/closure status
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS) / Stephen Mather Wilderness
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass at the Eldorado Creek Trailhead

The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado Creek Basin
bivy.notes: The usual first camp, about three miles and 3,300 ft from the car and the first flat, pretty ground after the long climb through timber and the boulder field. Camp on durable surfaces only — snow, rock or bare ground — and stay a hundred feet back from water; the meadow here is exactly what the rule is protecting. A comfortable planned camp, and the natural choice for parties who reach it late in the day.
bivy.water: Eldorado Creek and snowmelt through the basin, reliable
bivy.permit: A national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, reservable in advance and picked up at the ranger station in Marblemount
bivy.capacity: Open camping on rock and gravel benches — no built pads; the zone allows six parties a night, twelve people to a party

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin
bivy.notes: A higher alternative to the basin below, reached by climbing to the rocky ridge near 6,100 ft and dropping a few hundred feet down the far side. That drop has to be re-gained on the way out, which is the main argument against it, but it puts you closer to the glacier toe with water still running. A planned camp, not a bivy.
bivy.water: Reliable running water in the basin
bivy.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone
bivy.capacity: Open camping on the rib and in the basin, between roughly 6,100 and 6,400 ft

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier saddle high camp
bivy.notes: The best-positioned planned camp, on the broad flat apron where the glaciers meet, with the East Ridge and the summit knife-edge laid out in front of you. It is entirely exposed — no trees, no shelter, and weather arrives with nothing in the way. Both the Eldorado and the Inspiration carry real crevasse hazard that gets worse as the day warms, so you rope up before you reach camp and again when you leave it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only — bring a stove, there is nothing running at this height
bivy.permit: Same national park backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone. A composting toilet serves this camp; if you sleep away from it, human waste must go into blue bags and come out with you
bivy.capacity: Flat glacier apron and rock beside it, roughly 7,500-7,800 ft; the zone limit of six parties a night applies

access.fees: $10 per person per trip plus a $6 non-refundable Recreation.gov reservation fee for overnight wilderness permits (youth 15 and under free); no fee for a single-push, no-camp ascent.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the Mount Shuksan, Eldorado Peak and Forbidden Peak cross-country zones, which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Overnight parties need a wilderness permit for the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier cross-country zone, one of NOCA's busiest high-occupancy zones with a limited daily quota. Reserve on Recreation.gov, watch the mandatory backcountry safety video, and email noca_wilderness@nps.gov within 3 days of your trip; permits must be picked up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA 98267; (360) 854-7245) by 11am on the start date or the reservation is cancelled. A winter self-issue station is available when the WIC is closed. Camping is permitted on the Roush Creek rib (~5,400 ft) and the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier apron (~7,500 ft); camping in Eldorado Basin itself is prohibited due to heavy use.
access.closures: Cascade River Road typically opens to its upper trailheads by late June or early July after winter snow clears, and can be gated or washed out at various points (including near the Eldorado parking area at MP 20) after heavy rain — check NPS road-conditions updates before driving up.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the Mount Shuksan, Eldorado Peak and Forbidden Peak cross-country zones, which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry camping permit (required for any overnight stay; day climbs need none)
access.closures: Trailhead/road closed seasonally in winter (roughly Nov-June) at the Eldorado gate, mile 20; can also close early for flood or landslide damage
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No NW Forest Pass or interagency pass needed at the trailhead (it lies inside the park boundary past mile 18)

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come
