bivy.name: Bedal Basin, below the north side of Bedal Peak
bivy.notes: The high camp for BEDAL PEAK, sitting directly under its steep north side and its cliffs, and the only sensible place to sleep for a party attempting the peak rather than just visiting the basin. Getting here is about two and a half miles from the road end at around 2,800 ft, climbing steadily through old forest and across avalanche tracks, and the trail deteriorates as it goes — it receives very little maintenance, is thickly overgrown in the avalanche chutes by midsummer, and effectively gives out about a mile and a half in, after which the way is up the rocky creek bed and through thin forest into the basin. Expect brush, wet feet and route-finding rather than a walk. The basin holds the remains of a pioneer cabin among the boulders, which makes a useful landmark for orienting the last of the approach. The peak above needs route-finding and, on most lines, real climbing rather than scrambling, so the short approach should not be read as a short day. The spur road itself is the other constraint: two steep, rough miles where high clearance is genuinely wanted rather than merely advised. Bedal Campground sits a mile down the main loop road from the junction and is the drive-in fallback for a party that arrives too late to start up the spur, and it is already recorded in the earlier upper-loop file. Snow lies in the basin into July.
bivy.water: Bedal Creek and its meltwater feeders run through the basin and are reliable through the climbing season, thinning late in a hot August. The creek is crossed twice on the way up and both crossings are straightforward by midsummer but pushy in snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS, which begins about half a mile up the trail — free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the road end, no reservation and no quota, and a twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass to leave a vehicle. Fires are legal in principle at this elevation but inappropriate in a small meadow basin with limited dead wood, and summer restrictions usually prohibit them outright; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A meadow basin with room for several small parties on durable ground near the boulders, though flat spots are fewer than the open look of the place suggests. It is quiet — this trail sees very little traffic and you can have the basin to yourself on a summer weekend.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required at the FR 4096 trailhead - $5 day pass or $30 annual pass (Forest Service vendors/Recreation.gov).
access.rules: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness regulations apply above the wilderness boundary: no bikes or motorized/mechanized equipment, maximum group size 12, camp at least 200 ft from water and trails, pack out all trash and waste, Leave No Trace.
access.permit: No wilderness permit or quota currently required for day or overnight climbing; a self-issue trailhead register may be present.
access.closures: The unpaved 12-mile Mountain Loop Highway section between Barlow Pass and Bedal Campground, which FR 4096 branches off of, is gated and closed to vehicles roughly November through late May depending on snowpack, and has also seen multi-year closures after flood/washout damage. Confirm current status with the Darrington Ranger District (360-436-1155) or Snohomish County Public Works before relying on this access.'
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (Henry M. Jackson Wilderness).

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

bivy.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
bivy.notes: The climbing camp for KOLOLO PEAKS, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. Lower camps on the same approach sit at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
bivy.permit: GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/annual Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency Pass) required for parking at both the North Fork Sauk and White River trailheads
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead before entering Glacier Peak Wilderness (available at both the North Fork Sauk and White River/Indian Creek trailheads)
access.closures: A landslide closed the Mountain Loop Highway at milepost 37.5 (~15.5 mi south of Darrington) from December 2025, blocking vehicle access to FR 49 and the North Fork Sauk/Sloan Creek trailheads; repairs reopened the highway in mid-May 2026. Check Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before planning the west approach. Even when open, FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) has rough washout sections near miles 1 and 6; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (west/North Fork Sauk approach) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (east/White River approach) - both within Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: Mount Pugh road end, Forest Road 2095
bivy.notes: The staging point for MOUNT PUGH, which most parties climb in a single long day from here — around five and a half miles and well over five thousand feet to the summit, with the character changing three times on the way. Forest and stream crossings to the lake at a mile and a half, then a steady climb to the pass, then a rough exposed ridge with a genuine scrambling section around the head of a small remnant glacier before it eases to the top. Sleeping at the car is the honest plan for that day: the spur is short enough that a party staying at any of the valley campgrounds can drive up in the dark, and the trail's first miles are straightforward walking that goes quickly by headtorch. The spur climbs steeply and is rough in places but is normally passable to an ordinary car driven with care. The road in from Darrington is the county-maintained section of the loop and stays open through the year to the seasonal gate further south, which puts this trailhead on the right side of the winter closure — but it is landslide ground and has been blocked outright by a slide within recent memory, so confirm before driving from any distance rather than assuming. Season for the peak is roughly July into October; the ridge above the pass with snow on it is a mountaineering proposition rather than a scramble.
bivy.water: None at the road end and none for the first mile and a half of trail. Everything gets carried up from the valley or drawn at the lake above.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, and the trailhead itself sits OUTSIDE designated wilderness — Glacier Peak Wilderness begins high on the mountain above Stujack Pass, not at the road. Reports differ on whether a fee pass is enforced at this particular trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass costs nothing extra to carry and settles the question. No self-issue permit at the road. Seasonal forest-wide fire restrictions apply and from midsummer normally mean no open flame.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only, and a thin one. Parking is a few turnouts along the last of the spur rather than a car park, with no sites, no tables and no toilet. Half a dozen vehicles fills it and there is nowhere to overflow to without blocking the road.

bivy.name: Lake Metan, Mount Pugh trail
bivy.notes: A mile and a half and about thirteen hundred feet up from the road end, on a short signed spur off the main trail, this is the only established camping on the Pugh approach and it turns a punishing day into a manageable one. Its real value is for a party that wants the ridge above Stujack Pass in the cool of the morning without a two-hour drive and a headtorch start, or for one that arrives too late in the day to sensibly begin. It buys about a third of the climbing but leaves the hardest two thirds — a further two and a half miles to the pass and then the ridge — for the summit day, so treat it as a soft first night rather than a high camp. The setting is wooded and enclosed, mosquito-heavy in early summer and cold in the shade well into the morning. Snow lingers around the lake into June in an ordinary year. Because it is the last water, an efficient party often does not sleep here at all but stops for twenty minutes to load up, and that is a perfectly good use of the place.
bivy.water: The lake, and this is the LAST WATER on the entire route. Nothing above it is dependable, and above the pass there is nothing at all except late-lying snow. Fill everything here going up and note it for the descent.
bivy.permit: National forest outside designated wilderness at this elevation, so no wilderness permit, no quota and no party-size limit for camping here. A Northwest Forest Pass covers the vehicle. Fires are subject to whatever seasonal restrictions are in force and are usually prohibited from midsummer; carry a stove regardless, because this is a small lake basin that takes heavy day-hiker traffic and does not need fire rings.
bivy.capacity: A few primitive spots in the trees on the short spur down to the lake — two or three tents on flat, well-used forest ground, with no built structures of any kind.

bivy.name: Stujack Pass and the benches just below it
bivy.notes: This is a high bivouac rather than a camp, and it exists for one purpose — putting a party on the exposed upper ridge of MOUNT PUGH at first light rather than in the afternoon, when the scrambling section around the head of the small glacier is more pleasant and the weather is more predictable. From the saddle the remaining mile and a half of ridge is rough, narrow in places and genuinely exposed, and it is much better done rested and early than at the end of a five-thousand-foot day from the car. The trade is severe and should be weighed honestly: you carry all your water up, you camp on ground with nothing to hide behind, and the pass funnels wind hard enough to make a marginal forecast miserable. Anyone who is not committed to the summit is better off at the lake. Snow holds on the north side of the pass and in the gullies below it long after the trail lower down is clear, and an early-season party will be kicking steps to reach it. In a thunderstorm this is the wrong place to be — the ridge above is the highest ground for some way and there is no descent that is quick. Camp on gravel or bare rock, not on the heather, which is thin and slow to come back.
bivy.water: NONE, and this is the defining constraint. There is no source at or near the pass. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted early in the season and are gone by August, after which every litre comes up from the lake nearly two and a half miles and two and a half thousand feet below.
bivy.permit: The pass itself is the boundary — camping in the saddle sits at the very edge of GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, and the ridge and summit above are inside it. Where wilderness applies, so does the free self-issue permit from the trailhead box and the twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. No fires: this is thin subalpine ground with no wood and nothing that recovers from a scar. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a couple of tents at most on gravel and heather pockets in the saddle and on the shelves a little below it on the approach side. Nothing established, no flat platform, and no shelter of any kind from wind.

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.rules: Leave No Trace; the upper trail/scramble enters Glacier Peak Wilderness near Stujack Pass, where standard wilderness travel rules apply (no bikes or motorized equipment, group-size limits).
access.permit: None required

bivy.name: One Acre Lake, under Mount Stickney
bivy.notes: The one place worth camping on Mount Stickney, and the reason the peak is doable at all now that the road is gated low. The route leaves the Sultan Basin road onto the old Olney Creek logging road, which used to let a high-clearance vehicle grind up to around 2,100 feet and is now closed at its very beginning, so the road walk is five to six miles before any climbing starts. Where the road levels near 3,700 feet a trail cuts off to the right along a ridge; leave that around 4,050 feet and traverse southeast to the lake. From camp the route continues southeast past a set of tarns near 4,500 feet, up to about 4,800, and then traverses into the boulder basin below the summit, taking a gully just west of the top to gain the crest. THIS IS A WINTER AND EARLY SPRING PEAK by preference, not a summer one: the low western start means it comes into condition when everything else is buried, and deep snow covers a boulder field that is loose, awkward and slow when bare. The trade is that the same snow brings real avalanche exposure on the traverses above the lake, and early-season parties have found route-finding and slope assessment to be the hard part rather than the climbing. Expect a long day either way, and expect the road walk to feel longer on the way out.
bivy.water: The lake, and snowmelt in the drainages above it well into July. Treat everything; the basin is shallow and the water warms.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is outside the Wild Sky boundary on a mix of state and federal land. No pass at the gated roadhead. Fires are a poor idea in a basin this small and are restricted through most summers.
bivy.capacity: A few flat spots on the benches around a small tarn, informal and unimproved. Two or three tents.

bivy.name: Sultan Basin road pullouts and the Olney Creek gate
bivy.notes: A pure staging pullout for Mount Stickney, included because the road walk is now long enough that starting it at first light matters. From US 2 in Sultan, the Sultan Basin road runs north for roughly eleven and a half miles before the Olney Creek road turns off on the right, and the gate is at the very start of that turn. Sleeping at the gate saves an hour of driving in the dark and puts the five-to-six mile approach march in the coolest part of the morning. The Sultan Basin road is paved for its lower miles and gravel above; it is generally drivable in a normal car to the gate, but conditions after a wet winter are worth checking. This is working forest and watershed land rather than recreation land, so expect industrial traffic, expect gates to move, and do not count on a pullout being available where it was last year. There is no established camping anywhere between here and One Acre Lake.
bivy.water: Olney Creek, a short way along the closed road, where a spur drops to a bridge and a gravel bar. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Mixed state and municipal watershed land, with day-use restrictions posted in places and gates that change. Read the signs at the gate rather than assuming dispersed camping is permitted where you have parked. Fire restrictions here are usually stricter than on national forest and are enforced.
bivy.capacity: Gravel pullouts and a turnaround at the gate. Room to sleep in or beside a vehicle, nothing more. No toilet, no table, no fire ring you should trust.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass: $5 for a day pass or $30 for an annual pass, available at ranger stations, REI, or online.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness Act regulations apply within the Wild Sky Wilderness boundary: groups of 12 or fewer, no motorized or mechanized (including bike) travel once inside the wilderness boundary, Leave No Trace practices.
access.permit: No wilderness entry permit or self-issue system is required for Wild Sky Wilderness. A parking pass (Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency pass) is generally expected at Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF trailheads.
access.closures: The Olney Creek Road gate location has moved over the years — near mile 10-11 from the highway as of 2009, but in the 2020s parties describe it closed much closer to the Sultan Basin Road junction. Treat any specific older driving mileage as unreliable and check current conditions first.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Skykomish Ranger District — Wild Sky Wilderness (designated 2008).

bivy.name: Spire Mountain — the saddle northwest of the summit
bivy.notes: Spire Mountain has no established camping of any kind and most parties climb it in a single very long day, which is the honest answer. The route is entirely off-trail: leave the Index-Galena road at the snowplow turnaround just past the bridge, drop south into old forest, and fight through six hundred feet of steep ground choked with fallen timber before the slope becomes merely steep. Cliffs on the north end of the mountain are turned between about 4,200 and 4,400 feet, then a rising traverse southeast reaches open ground around 5,400 feet below the summit spire. The saddle above that, northwest of the true summit, is the only ground on the route flat enough to lie down on, and a party that has misjudged the day will end up there whether they planned to or not. From it the last three hundred feet are technical enough that most rope up for short exposed sections. ROAD STATUS IS THE LIMITING FACTOR: the Index-Galena road has repeatedly been cut by flood damage and bridge failure on the North Fork Skykomish, and when the bridge is out the road is simply not drivable from the Beckler River road, which adds many miles of walking to an approach that is already brutal. Confirm the road is open before committing to this peak. Best season is late July to early October, once the timber is dry and before the first storms make the traverse slabs greasy.
bivy.water: None. There is no water anywhere on this route once you leave the North Fork Skykomish at the road, and the saddle holds nothing but lingering snow patches into July. Carry everything, or melt snow early season.
bivy.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit required. Parking is a roadside pullout, so no forest pass is needed there.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on whatever flat ground the ridge crest offers. There is no established site here and nothing has been built.

bivy.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
bivy.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.
bivy.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year at the North Fork Skykomish Trailhead — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Recreation Pass, or the Forest Service's on-site digital 'Scan & Pay' all work; Washington's Discover Pass is NOT accepted here.
access.rules: Standard Wild Sky Wilderness rules apply: group size capped at 12 people/stock combined (larger groups must split and stay 1+ mile apart), no bikes or other mechanized/motorized equipment, camp stoves recommended over open fires, no cutting of standing trees/snags/boughs, pack out all trash.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead; no reservation or special-use permit needed beyond that for a day climb.
access.closures: As of mid-2026, both approach roads are washed out and access is effectively cut off: FR-63 (Index-Galena Road) has a major washout between mileposts 10-14 (Snohomish County Public Works estimates roughly $900,000 to repair) and is reported undrivable from the FR-65 side due to a North Fork Skykomish bridge/road failure; FR-65 (Beckler River Rd) itself is closed past Jack Pass (MP 12.3) due to downed trees and a washed-out bridge at the bottom of the valley. No confirmed reopening date at this writing — check the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF 'Road Damages/Closures - Skykomish District' alert page and call the Skykomish Ranger Station before planning a trip.

bivy.name: Gunn Basin, below Tailgunner Pass
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Tailgunner, and it turns a very long day into a comfortable one. The climbers' path leaves the Barclay Creek road below the Barclay Lake trailhead, crosses the creek, and then climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest on a faint boot track, with dirt-covered slabs, a narrow traverse under cliffs and an exposed crossing above a waterfall before the angle relents into the basin. Reckon on three to four hours to camp with overnight loads. From here Tailgunner itself is an easy hour of slabby scrambling, and Gunn Peak and Wing Peak are both within reach the same morning, which is the usual reason parties carry a camp up at all. The shoulder of Tailgunner holds a shallow tarn perched right on the lip of the drop, and it is the obvious place to put a tent, but it is exposed and there is nothing between it and the weather. Season is roughly July to early October; earlier than that the traverse under the cliffs holds hard snow and the waterfall crossing is genuinely dangerous. The approach path is not maintained, is easy to lose on the descent, and should be tracked on the way up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns in the basin through midsummer, and a small stream draining the pass. Both can dry to nothing by late August in a thin year — carry the day's water up from Barclay Creek if the season has been hot.
bivy.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit or quota for camping. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at the Barclay Lake trailhead and at the pullouts either side of it. Stoves rather than fires — the basin is at the edge of timberline and the scattered wood there is what holds the heather together.
bivy.capacity: Open heather benches and slabs holding perhaps three or four small tents, scattered rather than clustered. No constructed sites, no toilet, no fire ring worth using.

bivy.name: Barclay Creek roadhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is a staging camp rather than a destination, and it exists because the Tailgunner and Gunn climbers' path leaves the road here rather than at the lake. Sleeping at the roadhead lets a party start the steep forest climb in the dark and reach the basin before the day heats up, which matters on a south-facing approach. The spur road with the clearing drops off the main road a short distance below the pit toilet at the Barclay Lake trailhead; the path itself heads right before that clearing and is unsigned. Do not confuse this with Barclay Lake, which is a maintained walk-in with established lakeside sites and is covered elsewhere. The road is plowed nowhere and is gated by snow from roughly late November to April, which puts the winter ascent of Tailgunner well out of reach for most parties. Expect log trucks and weekend traffic through the summer, and expect the trailhead lot to be full by mid-morning on any fine Saturday.
bivy.water: Barclay Creek runs beside the road and is the only supply. Treat it.
bivy.permit: National forest, dispersed camping, no permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead parking itself. Campfire restrictions follow the district and are common from July onward — check before assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: A handful of rough dispersed pullouts and one small clearing on a spur road a short walk below the trailhead. Room for two or three vehicles to sleep beside, not a campground.

access.fees: $5 day-use fee at Barclay Lake Trailhead (Scan & Pay ePass) if you don't already hold an annual pass.
access.notes: Gunn Peak (immediately adjacent) is documented as the highest point of the Wild Sky Wilderness, confirming this peak cluster is within designated wilderness, not outside it.
access.rules: Wild Sky Wilderness rules apply: no motorized vehicles, bikes, or stock on Barclay Creek Trail; camp only in established sites; pack out all waste.
access.permit: No wilderness quota or self-issue permit system found for Wild Sky Wilderness; call the Skykomish Ranger District at (360) 677-2414 for current trail/creek-crossing conditions before you go.
access.closures: The footlog over Barclay Creek was removed for safety in spring 2026 with no announced replacement timeline, directly affecting the creek crossing used to reach Tailgunner Creek — check current conditions before heading out.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

bivy.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
bivy.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
bivy.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
bivy.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

bivy.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
bivy.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
bivy.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.

bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

bivy.name: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
bivy.notes: This is where a party climbing Wolframite from the Chewuch actually sleeps on the second night, and it matters because the arithmetic of the approach is punishing without it. The Tungsten Creek trail breaks off the Chewuch trail a little past eight miles and climbs steadily for about six more, with the creek on the left and the bulk of Wolframite ahead — so a party that has walked in from Thirtymile is looking at a long day before the climbing even begins. Breaking the climb here rather than pushing to the Boundary Trail junction puts you on running water, in shelter, and with the steep work done in the cool of the morning. It is also the sensible fallback when the ground at the junction is occupied by a horse party, which happens more often than the remoteness suggests. Expect burned forest in stretches, little shade, and blowdown that changes with every windstorm. Late July through September is the working season; snow holds on the north sides of the passes above into July.
bivy.water: Tungsten Creek runs alongside for the whole climb and is the dependable supply on this approach, holding into the autumn. THIS IS WHERE YOU FILL FOR THE SUMMIT, because the Boundary Trail crest above the junction runs on tarns and snowmelt and is unreliable by August, and the peak itself carries nothing. Old iron pipe from the mining days is scattered along the trail, which tells you where the workings took their water and not that any of it is usable now. Treat everything.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the easy one: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation and nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Thirtymile. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight — this is heavily used horse country. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer in this dry drainage and the wood is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the climb beside the creek, most taking one or two tents, with the better ground in the lower half where the timber is still standing. Nothing developed and no facilities, and you are unlikely to meet anyone.

bivy.name: The Boundary Trail horse camp east of the Tungsten junction
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for a party climbing Wolframite and then continuing east along the Boundary Trail toward Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Basin, which is the classic way to use this corridor — the summits along it are all short detours off the trail with very little gain, and Wolframite is the first of them. Being a mile east of the junction it sits below the peak's south-east side rather than directly under the west approach, so a party going in and straight back out is better served staying at the mine junction ground or lower on Tungsten Creek. Its real value is that it is prepared, level and used, on a crest where most of the camping is improvised. THE WEST SIDE IS THE ROUTE. From the junction the Boundary Trail is followed roughly a mile west to where it turns south for Apex Pass, and the peak is climbed off-trail to the north-east up gentle open slopes; taken well this is easy scrambling, and taken badly it puts you on short steps of harder rock for no reason. Pick the line from below in good light rather than committing to the first gully you meet.
bivy.water: Seasonal and worth checking rather than assuming. There is water at the site early in the year and it becomes unreliable as the summer goes on, in common with everything on this crest — parties have found streams dry and pools with cracked bottoms along this trail in September. Carry up from Tungsten Creek if you are arriving late in the season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Camp on the existing bare ground. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are the norm here by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: An established site roughly a mile east of the junction with the Tungsten Creek trail, laid out with horse feed in mind, so it takes a stock party comfortably and a walking party easily. One of very few genuinely prepared camps along this stretch of the Boundary Trail.

bivy.name: Apex Pass and the high ground west of Wolframite
bivy.notes: The pass is where the Boundary Trail bends south a mile west of the Wolframite approach, and it is the link between this peak and the Cathedral country — Apex Mountain stands immediately above it, Amphitheater and Cathedral Peak are further west, and a party collecting summits along this crest will pass through here whichever direction they are travelling. As a camp it is bought and paid for in water and wind: the position is superb and the ground gives no protection at all. Its argument is position rather than comfort, since from here Wolframite is a short morning to the east and Apex is a short morning above. WHAT IT IS NOT is a substitute for a lower camp on a first night — a party arriving here tired and dry has made the trip harder, not easier. Snow lies on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much longer after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when the crest is worth traversing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights up here are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and the odd tarn early in the season, and frequently nothing at all by late summer. This is a place you carry water to, not one you collect at. The last dependable source coming up is Tungsten Creek; coming from the Cathedral side it is the lake basins, which are a long way west. A party that has not carried enough will be walking a long way down for it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota, no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at whichever trailhead you used. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this height and the alpine turf is fragile enough that a footprint lasts years, so pitch on gravel or rock.
bivy.capacity: Open alpine ground at and around the pass with room for a small party or two on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind from wind.

bivy.name: Teapot Lake and the Boundary Trail benches toward Bauerman Ridge
bivy.notes: The eastern half of the Wolframite corridor, and the camp for a party crossing between this peak and the Horseshoe Basin country rather than going in and out from the Chewuch. It is roughly fourteen miles of mild, high walking from the Tungsten junction east to Horseshoe Basin, staying largely above seven thousand feet, with Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Mountain all coming off the trail as short detours in the same way Wolframite does. THIS TRAVERSE IS DECIDED BY WATER AND NOT BY DISTANCE. In a dry September the crest carries almost nothing, and parties have walked it past empty pools and dry streambeds with this lake and the occasional trickle as the only supply — which turns a gentle high walk into a rationing exercise. Plan the days around the sources rather than around the miles, fill at every one, and treat any pool as suspect. The far end of this line is the Iron Gate trailhead above Toats Coulee, whose last six miles of road want high clearance, and whose Horseshoe Basin camps are recorded in the eastern Pasayten file rather than here.
bivy.water: Teapot Lake is the dependable one on this stretch and that is precisely why parties camp at it rather than on the ridge — but it is a small standing body and has been found stagnant in a dry year, so treat it properly and take it from an inlet if there is one running. The streams and pools between here and the Wolframite junction go dry through the season and cannot be counted on.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from whichever trailhead kiosk you started at, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, but there is little to burn and the ground is thin.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and on the benches either side of the trail, room for a party or two at each. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and long odds against meeting anyone.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/annual at Thirtymile Trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful), or Digital Day Pass all honored.
access.rules: Standard wilderness group-size and Leave No Trace rules apply. The Tungsten Mine site's remaining structures are maintained through volunteer trail-crew work by groups such as the Pacific Northwest Trail Association, Washington Trails Association, and Back Country Horsemen of Washington, coordinated with the US Forest Service — do not disturb buildings, equipment, or artifacts. Food storage precautions are worth taking; the area sees black bear, cougar, and wolf activity, and lies within the North Cascades grizzly bear recovery zone.
access.permit: Free, self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit completed at the trailhead — no advance reservation or fee for the wilderness permit itself.
access.closures: No standing closure found for this specific route as of research; FR 51 (Chewuch River Road) is a long gravel forest road that can have early-season snow or washout issues — check current conditions with the Methow Valley Ranger District before driving in.
